fields.label: 2-Minute Summary Overview
fields.value: Postmodern literature is a form of literature which is marked, both stylistically and ideologically, by a reliance on such literary conventions as fragmentation, paradox, unreliable narrators, often unrealistic and downright impossible plots, games, parody, paranoia, dark humor and authorial self-reference. Postmodern authors tend to reject outright meanings in their novels, stories and poems, and, instead, highlight and celebrate the possibility of multiple meanings, or a complete lack of meaning, within a single literary work.

fields.label: 2-Minute Summary Overview
fields.value: The Jindyworobak movement was an Australian literary movement of 1930's and 1940's whose white members, mostly poets, sought to contribute to a uniquely Australian culture through the integration of Indigenous Australian Subjects, language and mythology. The aim of the movement was - "to free Australian art from whatever alien influences trammel it", and "create works based on an understanding of Australia's history and tradition, primeval, colonial and modern".

fields.label: 2-Minute Summary Overview
fields.value: 'Realism' was a style and type of writing that emerged during 1865-1910 in American Literary history when writers sought to portray life as it really was: real characters in real lives, with real jobs and real problems. Realism was a reaction to and rejection of Romanticism.

fields.value: New Criticism was a formalist movement in literary theory in US, that dominated American Literary criticism in the middle decades of 20th century. It is opposite of Reader Response Theory. It emphasized close reading particularly of poetry to discover how a work of literature functioned as a self contained, self-referential aesthetic object. For New Critics - "a poem is a well-wrought urn."

fields.label: 2-Minute Summary Overview
fields.value: Second Language Acquisition or Second Language Learning is the process by which people, learn second language. It is a sub-discipline of applied linguistics. The central theme of SLA research is that of Inter language, the idea that the language that learners use is not simply the result of difference between the languages that they already know and the language that they are learning, but that it is a complete language system in its own right with its own systematic rules.

fields.label: 2-Minute Summary Overview
fields.value: 1. Broken Rhyme : This is where one rhyming word or words matches up with a piece of another. e.g. Meeting - Proposal Exceptional - Shall Win Suppose - Lover Coverlet - Deception 2. Chain Rhyme : A rhyme scheme in which a rhyme in a line of one stanza is used as a link to a rhyme in the next stanza. 3. Cross Rhyme : The rhyme of each stanza is called cross rhyme when the syllable at the end of a line rhymes with a word in the middle of a line before or after it. e.g. The Sound flung on the air, the song is sung. (Here flung and sung are cross rhymes). 4. Dialect Rhyme : Rhyme that depends on pronunciation based on historical period or region. e.g. Again - Pair vs Again Pen. 5. Di-syllabic Rhyme : A rhyme in which the two last syllables of words share the same sound. e.g. - Emotion, Motion 6. End Rhymes (Sight Rhyme) : The near duplication of sounds that takes place at the end of lines. It is most common type of rhyme. e.g. Heat, Neat , Feet, Greet, Sweet 7. Eye Rhyme : Rhyme in which the endings of words are spelled alike; in most instances were pronounced alike, but not always they are pronounced alike. 8. Feminine Rhyme : A rhyme that occurs when the final syllable in unstressed (normally used with multi - syllable words) for example - Pleasure/ Leisure Longing/ Yearning 9. Forced Rhymes (Wrenched Rhyme): It occurs when the poet gives the effect of seeming to surrender helplessly to the exigencies of a difficult rhyme. e.g. Farewell, Farewell, You old rhinoceros I'll stare at something less preposterous. 10. Forced Rhyme : A rhyme that is produced by changing the normal spelling of a word, or by changing the normal structure of a phrase. e.g. - The cat crossed the grass. I was late for class. 11. Head Rhyme Rhyme between syllables at the beginning of lines of poetry. e.g. Sung is the song Flung upon the air (Sung and Flung are head rhymes) 12. Imperfect Rhyme (Partial, Half, Near, Off Slant, or Approximate Rhyme): A Rhyme in which the vowels are either approximate or different; and occasionally, even the rhymed consonants are similar rather than identical. e.g. - Dry, Died (i)
